heading: Choose a service language
body: A service is a file client/services/<Name>Service.js, .ts or .dart. You can also write it as <Name>Service.rs, .go, .rb, .swift, .kt, .cs or .fs in the same folder. A component holds only its tac.html and tac.css. A page holds only its own tac.html, which places components. JavaScript and TypeScript run on every target. Dart compiles to WebAssembly with garbage collection (WasmGC), which ships wherever that bundle ships (ADR 0033; an ADR is an architecture decision record). WasmGC needs Chrome or Edge 119, Firefox 120 or Safari 18.2 and newer; an older browser shows a clear error instead of the Dart or Kotlin services. A Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift or Kotlin service with no browser sibling compiles to WebAssembly. It runs as WebAssembly on the web and on any target that does not link it (ADR 0035, ADR 0037, ADR 0045, ADR 0073, ADR 0078, ADR 0082). Kotlin compiles to WasmGC, like Dart, so it needs the same browsers. When a service has files in several of these languages, Tachyon uses the first one in this order: Rust, Go, C#, Swift, Kotlin, Ruby. A release build makes the Kotlin program about three times smaller with Binaryen, as Kotlin's own production build does. Every other WebAssembly language also gets the compiler and settings that make the smallest download: TinyGo for Go, a size-tuned rustc for Rust, -Osize and Binaryen for Swift, a trimmed .NET interpreter for C# and F#, and -O4 for Dart (see WebAssembly compilers per language). A Swift program holds the Swift standard library, about 3.4 MB (0.9 MB with Brotli), so a Swift web service should not import Foundation, which would make it more than ten times larger. It does not need it: models in client/models cross the page boundary through Codable, with an encoder and decoder that Tachyon ships in the Swift program. No target links Go, so a Go service runs as WebAssembly on every target. A Ruby service runs on Tachyon's mruby WebAssembly runtime on every target (ADR 0054). Your machine builds that runtime once with Ruby and Emscripten. Native services link on their supported targets: Rust on desktop, Swift on Apple, Kotlin on Android and C# on Windows. On every other target they run as WebAssembly, so every service language reaches every target. Python, PHP and Groovy are not Tac service languages, so this site, which has no server, has no service in them. This site is a complete example of the web mix, with two or three services in each language. Rust holds the contents list and page links. Go holds the feature catalogue and the inline code in prose. Ruby holds the navigation drawer and the code showcase. C# holds the documentation index and the list of Yon examples. F# holds the choice of install command on the home page and the counts of the documentation index, such as "1 feature" or "12 features". Dart holds the sidebar and pager. Kotlin holds the reading time and the place in the reading order of each guide. Swift holds the word and group filters of the feature list. TypeScript holds the clipboard, platform choice and guide pages. JavaScript holds the feature pages, search and code examples. A page loads the runtime of a language only when one of its views uses a service in that language, so the Swift program (about 0.9 MB with Brotli) loads only on the feature list. A unit test in the same language tests each service. Content that is only data is not a service at all. Examples are the pillars, FAQ, footer and quickstart. This content lives in client/shared/data, and a view reads it as data.<name> (ADR 0036).
